Job levels describe how senior a role is. Job families describe what kind of work it does. Most compensation decisions need both, and mixing them up is where benchmarking goes wrong.


As a compensation professional, you know there’s *a lot* of terminology to wrap your head around. Sometimes it’s helpful to get a quick refresher on the basics.


Here, we’re breaking down the ins and outs of a few key terms, job levels, job tracks, and job families, including what each one means and how job level classification works in practice. We’ll also share how job levels and families set the foundation for[compensation benchmarking](https://www.pave.com/s/salary-benchmarking) .


## What is a job level?


A job level refers to the seniority, experience, and scope of responsibility of a role. That is the job level meaning in one line, and it is the same idea some organizations call career levels or grades.


Job levels are often broken down further by:


- **Job track** : This indicates whether an employee is an individual contributor or a people manager. Larger and more complex businesses may also create more detailed job tracks for different organizational functions, such as sales or customer support.


- **Experience level:** This is often categorized as a number on a scale of 1-10, with 1 being the most junior level and 10 being the most senior.


Job levels typically vary by organization. The degree of job-level granularity depends on a company’s complexity and growth stage. Smaller companies often have broader job level categories, while larger companies may add more layers to their job levels.


How deep a ladder runs comes down to three things: how big the company is, what stage it is at, and which function you are looking at.[Pave data](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/how-many-direct-reports-is-too-many-exploring-the-management-track) shows small companies working with one or two manager levels, and the ladder lengthening from there. The examples below show what that looks like in practice, on both the manager and the individual contributor track.


### Manager levels in software engineering


On the management track, early-stage companies run a median of two manager job levels in software engineering, a fintech peer group runs five, and technology companies with more than 3,000 employees run six.

### Individual contributor levels in software engineering


The individual contributor ladder stretches the same way and usually runs longer. The median software engineering ladder is five levels at an early-stage company, seven across a fintech peer group, and eight at technology companies with more than 3,000 employees.

### Individual contributor levels in sales


Sales runs shallower at the start and catches up at scale, with a median of four levels at early-stage companies, six across a fintech peer group, and eight at large technology companies.

Generally, compensation data and survey providers group levels into a handful of tracks, with four levels for management and six for professionals or individual contributors. Not every company will use every level, and that depends on size and stage. Source: Pave. Levels on the same row of the framework carry equivalent seniority, which is why the executive track sits above the management track and the support track alongside the lower professional levels.


## What is a job family?


A job family refers to a functional group within an organization, such as accounting, sales, marketing, or customer success. The roles within a job family involve similar work and skills.


Within job families, there are job sub-families, which add more specificity to roles.


For example, within the accounting job family, there may be the following sub-families:


- Accounting – generalist
- Accounts payable/receivable
- Controller
- Invoice operations
- Payroll


You can find a complete breakdown of[Pave job families and sub-families here.](https://www.pave.com/products/market-data-job-catalog)


Much like job levels, job families can vary in complexity and granularity.


Source: alamere.io


For example, at[Pave’s Total Rewards Live event](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/the-top-4-compensation-strategy-takeaways-from-total-rewards-live) , we hosted a panel about the trends in AI and Machine Learning (ML) engineering, and how these roles differ from Software Engineers. We learned that about half of the attendees group[AI and ML engineers](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/hiring-for-ai-engineers-is-on-the-rise-is-your-compensation-strategy-ready) into the software engineering job family, while the other half have a standalone ML job family.


Many smaller organizations take a more straightforward approach to job families, while larger companies often incorporate additional granularity.

## Why do job levels and job families matter for compensation benchmarking?


These[salary ranges](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/what-is-a-salary-range-guide) impact the entire organization, helping to establish the foundation for fair compensation, control labor costs, and give teams an edge in a competitive labor market.


Once comp leaders have defined their job levels, tracks, and families, they can start gathering compensation data and building[salary bands](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/salary-bands) against it. We recommend using sources such as:


- **Real-time data** : You can use[Pave’s free benchmarking tool](https://www.pave.com/benchmarking) to quickly access compensation benchmarks from over 9,000 companies.


- **Offer data** : Pave partnered with Greenhouse to bring you[real-time offer data](https://www.pave.com/offer-insights) , trends, and insights into salary and acceptance rates.


- **Compensation surveys** : Survey data providers like Aon Radford and Willis Towers Watson provide high-quality job family data.


Aggregating multiple data sources enables you to define more accurate salary ranges and set robust compensation benchmarks.

### **Frequently asked questions**


##### **What are job levels?**


Job levels are the tiers a company uses to describe how senior a role is, based on experience, scope of responsibility, and decision-making authority. Most compensation providers use four levels for managers and six for individual contributors, and companies use as many of those as their size warrants.


##### **What is the job level definition?**


A job level is a defined step of seniority within a job family. It sets what the role is expected to own, what experience it assumes, and which pay range applies. Levels are what make two roles in different departments comparable.


##### **How does job level classification work?**


You define the levels, then assign each role to one by comparing scope, impact, and required expertise against the level criteria. The output is a consistent structure you can benchmark against, which is why leveling has to be settled before market pricing. The mechanics of building that structure are covered in our[job leveling matrix](https://www.pave.com/blog-posts/job-leveling-framework) guide.


##### **What is the difference between a job level and a job family?**


A job level is vertical and a job family is horizontal. The level says how senior the role is, the family says what kind of work it does. Software Engineer II and Account Executive II sit at comparable levels in different families.
